extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers / creative writers (short story and novel authors) interested in craft and revision
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for ensuring every prominent element introduced in a story serves a narrative purpose (i.e., is planted and paid off). Useful for plotting, foreshadowing, and revision decisions in fiction writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity Principle (Chekhov's Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you say in the first act that there is a rifle hanging on the wall, in the second or third act it absolutely must go off. If it's not going to be fired, it shouldn't be hanging there." — Anton Chekhov
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every prominent element introduced in a story must serve a purpose. Irrelevant details that accumulate but never pay off violate an implicit promise to the reader. If an element is presented (foregrounded or emphasized), ensure it has a payoff later or remove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical object as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical object (Chekhov's literal example)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects that receive attention (a rifle, a key, a letter) must be used or have narrative significance later; otherwise they create a broken promise to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character trait or personality quirk as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: A character trait or personality quirk introduced
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits or quirks that are emphasized should influence choices, plot outcomes, or theme; if they have no effect on the story, consider removing or reworking them so they contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of backstory mentioned
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backstory presented to the reader should matter to the present action or character arcs; extraneous backstory that never affects the plot violates the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line of dialogue as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: A line of dialogue with apparent significance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lines that are made to feel significant (repeated, emphasized, or framed) should connect to later events or revelations; avoid throwaway lines framed as important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentioned skill as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: A skill the protagonist mentions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skills introduced (e.g., marksmanship, lockpicking) should plausibly be used or influence the climax/resolution; if not, either remove the mention or revise so the skill matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresolved problem/conflict as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: An unresolved problem or conflict
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts or problems that are introduced and foregrounded should be addressed or resolved in a meaningful way; leaving them irrelevant breaks the reader's expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowed event as a 'gun'
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreshadowed event
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that are foreshadowed should pay off in a way that feels earned; planting earlier clues makes later events feel satisfying rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every emphasized element pays off
rubrics_metrics.description: Every emphasized element pays off
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you draw attention to something—through description, repetition, or narrative focus—the reader will expect it to have significance; ensure payoff or remove emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foregrounding signals importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Foregrounding signals importance — the reader expects significance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that narrative framing (placement, description, emphasis) signals importance. Use foregrounding intentionally to create valid expectations and then fulfill them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red herrings must be intentional
rubrics_metrics.description: "Red herrings" must be intentional misdirection, not laziness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you include misleading elements, they should be crafted as deliberate misdirection that serves plot or theme; accidental or lazy red herrings frustrate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut what doesn't pay off in revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut what doesn't pay off in revision
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During revision, ask whether each element has a purpose; remove or repurpose details that make promises you don't keep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing requirement (inverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an event to feel earned at the climax, it should be planted earlier. The "gun" must have been hung on the wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid climaxes feeling arbitrary, seed necessary information, skills, or objects early enough that later resolutions are plausible and satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: loaded objects that never fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Loaded objects that never fire (broken promise)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects presented as significant that never affect the plot constitute a broken promise; identify and fix or remove such elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: mentioned skills not used
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills mentioned in act 1 that aren't used at climax
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing abilities or competencies that are never utilized; either use them in the resolution or omit the mention to prevent reader frustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: irrelevant backstory
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory introduced that doesn't matter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim backstory that doesn't influence character motivation, plot, or theme—if it doesn't matter, it clutters the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: coincidences without setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences that don't follow from setup
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist resolving plot with unexplained coincidences; ensure outcomes follow from established setup or character action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure mode: deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Climaxes solved by previously unmentioned tools/abilities (deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing solutions at the last minute that have not been signaled earlier; such devices undermine payoff and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension with realism — selectivity of fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Real life has many irrelevant details; fiction is selective. Chekhov's gun acknowledges this — fiction is a designed system, not a transcript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principle to justify selective representation: unlike real life, fiction should only present details that bear on the narrative, because what's shown creates reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension with Hemingway's Iceberg Theory (compatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hemingway's iceberg suggests more unsaid than said. Chekhov's gun says: what is said must matter. Both compatible: the iceberg is what you know but don't show; the gun is what you show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can keep rich unseen context (the iceberg) while ensuring that whatever you choose to show (the gun) has narrative purpose. Don't conflate unsaid depth with irrelevant on-page details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality tests checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Why is this detail in this story? What promise does it make? Is that promise kept? Could the story exist without this element? If yes, cut it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four diagnostic questions during revision to evaluate elements: 1) Why is this detail in this story? 2) What promise does it make? 3) Is that promise kept? 4) Could the story exist without this element? If the answer to the last is yes, consider cutting.
